assessments.reasoning: The I/O paper’s abstract assigns common file operations and buffer management to a logical layer. The Design Overview explicitly describes Lisp code for buffer assignment and stream state, and separates the abstract interface from lower-level physical devices.

challenge.method: Read the later abstract-device section and its dispatch and CORE examples to test whether the logical layer or uniform interface implies a common driver, byte-stream operation at the device, or a pure physical disk model.
challenge.results: The layer supplies buffer and stream services above per-device operations. Devices may implement a common abstraction with distinct code and optional device-specific operations. A main-memory CORE example also makes the abstract device boundary concrete without changing the scoped layer proposition.

limitations: The review is architectural and documentary. It did not exercise a historical I/O system or generalize the design to every Interlisp implementation.
